chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Malik ibn Atiyya, from some of the companions of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) came out to us while he was angry, and he said: 'I had just gone out for a need, and some of the black people of Medina presented themselves to me and shouted at me, saying:
Here I am (Labbaik), O Ja'far ibn Muhammad, here I am!

So I returned back to my house, fearful and panicked from what they had said, until I prostrated to my Lord in my mosque, rubbed my face to Him, humbled myself to Him, and distanced myself to Him from what they had shouted at me.

And if Isa ibn Maryam had added anything to what Allah said regarding him, then he would have become deaf and would not have been able to hear anything after that ever, and become blinded and would not have been able to see anything after that ever, and become dumb and would not have been able to speak anything after that ever.
Then he said: 'May Allah curse Abu al-Khattab and kill him with the iron.'

key_terms.لَبَّيْكَ: Here I am / Responding (a term of respect or response)

ai.seo_question: What is the story of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq's anger and the meaning of 'Labbaik' in this hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the Imam’s sensitivity to subtle shifts in status and the potential for *ghuluw* (exaggeration) by his followers, specifically the Ghulat sect of Abu al-Khattab. The Imam’s reaction—returning home in fear to prostrate and seek forgiveness—highlights the Shia theological emphasis on maintaining humility and distinguishing between respectful address and divine attribution. His reference to Jesus (Isa) serves as a comparative baseline for prophetic humility, while his specific curse on Abu al-Khattab links this incident to the historical context of the Ghulat’s elevation of the Imams to near-divine status.
